name: Core Git
description: Protects against destructive git commands that can lose uncommitted work, \ rewrite history, or destroy stashes

destructive_patterns.name: git-alias-semantic-unverified
destructive_patterns.description: The invoked Git alias depends on shell expansion, contains a cycle, or exceeds the engine's bounded semantic analysis.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Review the fully expanded Git executable, alias chain, shell-alias body, and appended arguments before allowing execution. Dynamic shell values, cycles, and commands beyond the semantic parser's bounds can hide destructive operations.

destructive_patterns.name: branch-dynamic-token
destructive_patterns.description: A dynamic shell expansion in this git branch command can expand into a deletion or forced ref update. Quote the branch name or add `--` to make it a literal creation.

destructive_patterns.name: checkout-discard
destructive_patterns.description: git checkout -- discards uncommitted changes permanently. Use 'git stash' first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git checkout -- <path> discards all uncommitted changes to the specified files \ in your working directory. These changes are permanently lost - they cannot be \ recovered because they were never committed.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git stash: Save changes temporarily, restore later with 'git stash pop' \ - git diff <path>: Review what would be lost before discarding

\ Preview changes first: git diff -- <path>

\ Recovering from a failed `git pull --rebase`? \ Run `rv allow-once` in this repo, then retry the command. This issues a \ short-lived, single-shot permit that unblocks this rule only. A rebase already \ in progress (`.git/rebase-merge/` or `.git/rebase-apply/` present) auto-allows \ the same rule without a permit.

destructive_patterns.name: checkout-ref-discard
destructive_patterns.description: git checkout <ref> -- <path> overwrites working tree. Use 'git stash' first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git checkout <ref> -- <path> replaces your working tree files with versions from \ another commit or branch. Any uncommitted changes to those files are permanently \ lost - they cannot be recovered.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git stash: Save changes first, then checkout, then restore with 'git stash pop' \ - git show <ref>:<path>: View the file content without overwriting

\ Preview what would change: git diff HEAD <ref> -- <path>

destructive_patterns.name: restore-worktree
destructive_patterns.description: git restore discards uncommitted changes. Use 'git stash' or 'git diff' first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git restore <path> discards uncommitted changes in your working directory, \ reverting files to their last committed state. Changes that were never \ committed are permanently lost.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git restore --staged <path>: Only unstage, keeps working directory changes \ - git stash: Save all changes temporarily \ - git diff <path>: Review what would be lost

\ Preview changes first: git diff <path>

\ Recovering from a failed `git pull --rebase`? \ Run `rv allow-once` in this repo, then retry the command. This issues a \ short-lived, single-shot permit that unblocks this rule only. A rebase already \ in progress (`.git/rebase-merge/` or `.git/rebase-apply/` present) auto-allows \ the same rule without a permit.

destructive_patterns.name: restore-worktree-explicit
destructive_patterns.description: git restore --worktree/-W discards uncommitted changes permanently.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git restore --worktree (or -W) explicitly targets your working directory, \ discarding uncommitted changes. Even when combined with --staged, the worktree \ changes are permanently lost.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git restore --staged <path>: Only unstage, keeps working directory \ - git stash: Save changes first

\ Preview changes first: git diff <path>

destructive_patterns.name: reset-hard
destructive_patterns.description: git reset --hard destroys uncommitted changes. Use 'git stash' first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git reset --hard discards ALL uncommitted changes in your working directory \ AND staging area. This is one of the most dangerous git commands because \ changes that were never committed cannot be recovered by any means.

\ What gets destroyed: \ - All modified files revert to the target commit \ - All staged changes are lost \ - Untracked files remain (use git clean to remove those)

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git reset --soft <ref>: Move HEAD but keep all changes staged \ - git reset --mixed <ref>: Move HEAD, unstage changes, keep working dir (default) \ - git stash: Save changes before resetting

\ Preview what would be lost: git status && git diff

destructive_patterns.name: reset-merge
destructive_patterns.description: git reset --merge can lose uncommitted changes.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git reset --merge resets the index and updates files in the working tree that \ differ between the target commit and HEAD, but keeps changes that are not staged. \ However, if there are uncommitted changes in files that need to be updated, \ those changes will be lost.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git stash: Save uncommitted changes before reset \ - git merge --abort: If in the middle of a merge, abort safely

\ Preview what would change: git status && git diff

destructive_patterns.name: clean-force
destructive_patterns.description: git clean -f/--force removes untracked files permanently. Review with 'git clean -n' first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git clean -f permanently deletes untracked files from your working directory. \ These are files that have never been committed to git, so they cannot be \ recovered from git history. If you haven't backed them up elsewhere, they \ are gone forever.

\ Common dangerous combinations: \ - git clean -fd: Also removes untracked directories \ - git clean -xf: Also removes ignored files (build artifacts, .env, etc.)

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git clean -n: Dry-run, shows what would be deleted \ - git clean -i: Interactive mode, choose what to delete

\ ALWAYS preview first: git clean -n -d

destructive_patterns.name: push-force-long
destructive_patterns.description: Force push can destroy remote history. Use --force-with-lease if necessary.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git push --force overwrites remote history with your local history. This can \ permanently destroy commits that others have already pulled, causing data loss \ for your entire team. Collaborators may lose work, and recovering requires \ manual intervention from everyone affected.

\ What can go wrong: \ - Commits others pushed are deleted from remote \ - Team members get diverged histories \ - CI/CD pipelines may reference deleted commits

\ Safer alternative: \ - git push --force-with-lease: Only forces if remote matches your last fetch

\ Check remote state first: git fetch && git log origin/<branch>..HEAD

destructive_patterns.name: push-force-short
destructive_patterns.description: Force push (-f) can destroy remote history. Use --force-with-lease if necessary.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git push -f (short for --force) overwrites remote history with your local history. \ This can permanently destroy commits that others have already pulled, causing data \ loss for your entire team.

\ What can go wrong: \ - Commits others pushed are deleted from remote \ - Team members get diverged histories \ - CI/CD pipelines may reference deleted commits

\ Safer alternative: \ - git push --force-with-lease: Only forces if remote matches your last fetch

\ Check remote state first: git fetch && git log origin/<branch>..HEAD

destructive_patterns.name: branch-force-delete
destructive_patterns.description: git branch deletion or forced ref updates require explicit user approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git branch -d, -D, or --delete removes a branch reference. Lowercase -d \ checks that Git considers the branch merged, but it still discards the branch \ name, tracking configuration, and convenient reflog reference. The user may \ intentionally need any of those. The -f/--force forms can also move an existing \ branch reference away from commits. Agents must not cross either user-intent \ boundary without explicit approval. The -M and -C shorthands force-overwrite an \ existing rename/copy target and require the same approval.

\ Review without changing refs: \ - git branch -vv: Show branch tips and upstream tracking state \ - git branch --merged / --no-merged: Review Git's merge classification \ - git log --oneline --decorate <branch>: Inspect the branch history

\ Recovery if deletion already happened: \ git reflog # Find the commit hash while it is still retained \ git branch <branch> <commit-hash>

destructive_patterns.name: stash-drop
destructive_patterns.description: git stash drop deletes a single stash. Recoverable via `git fsck` (unreachable objects).
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git stash drop removes a specific stash entry from your stash list. The stashed \ changes become unreferenced but remain in git's object database temporarily. \ They can often be recovered using git fsck, but this is not guaranteed and \ becomes harder over time as git garbage collects.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git stash pop: Apply and drop in one step (only drops if apply succeeds) \ - git stash apply: Apply without dropping, verify first

\ Recovery if needed: \ git fsck --unreachable | grep commit \ git show <commit-hash> # Inspect each to find your stash

destructive_patterns.name: stash-clear
destructive_patterns.description: git stash clear permanently deletes ALL stashed changes.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
git stash clear removes ALL stash entries at once. Unlike git stash drop, \ which removes one at a time, this command wipes your entire stash list. \ All stashed changes become unreferenced and are very difficult to recover.

\ What gets destroyed: \ - All entries in 'git stash list' are removed \ - Multiple sets of saved work-in-progress may be lost

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git stash drop stash@{n}: Remove one specific stash at a time \ - git stash list: Review what would be lost first \ - git stash show stash@{n}: Inspect each stash before deciding

\ Recovery (difficult, not guaranteed): \ git fsck --unreachable | grep commit
